query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a thin reactive hafnium coating on refractory high-entropy alloys will enhance their high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a dense, adherent HfO2-rich protective scale.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys that, in the untreated state, form rapid, non-protective oxide scales when exposed to extreme high-temperature oxygen environments.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a thin reactive hafnium coating on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Oxidation testing at approximately 1200°C in an air atmosphere for around 100 hours to simulate extreme service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin Hf-rich surface layer that oxidizes to form a coherent HfO2 protective scale, potentially interacting with diffusing elements (e.g., Zr) to develop a transition layer that further improves scale adhesion.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the reactive Hf coating oxidizes to form a stable, dense HfO2 layer. This layer acts as a barrier by reducing oxygen diffusion and retarding further oxidation of the underlying alloy. The improved adhesion of the oxide scale limits spallation and provides enhanced oxidation resistance compared to the untreated state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, the Hf-coated samples will exhibit a significantly lower weight gain per unit area and a more intact, adherent oxide scale after exposure to 1200°C in air for 100 hours.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA that exhibits rapid oxidation with non-protective oxide scale formation under the specified extreme-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for refractory HEAs used in high-temperature structural applications; however, its success depends on factors like coating uniformity, accurate thickness control, and compatibility with specific substrate compositions. Its performance may vary under different environmental conditions or alloy chemistries.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., percentage reduction in oxidation rate or weight gain) is uncertain and requires experimental validation under the specified conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples. One set will receive a uniformly deposited thin reactive hafnium coating, while the other set remains uncoated. Expose both sets to an air atmosphere at 1200°C for 100 hours. Post-exposure, assess each sample’s oxidation behavior.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area via precision gravimetry
Oxide scale thickness, morphology, and continuity using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS)
Adhesion and integrity of the oxide scale assessed via microstructural analysis and appropriate adhesion tests (e.g., scratch or pull-off tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in weight gain per unit area and do not show improved scale continuity and adhesion compared to the untreated samples under the test conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Ultra-high Temperature Oxidation-Resistant Alloys (UTORAs) have received a lot of attention due to the increased research demand for deep space exploration around the world. However, UTORAs have the disadvantages of easy oxidation and chalking. So, in this study, a UTORAs is prepared by hot-press sintering on VZrHfNbTa (HEA: High Entropy Alloys can generally be defined as more than five elements by the equal atomic ratio or close to the equal atomic ratio alloying, the mixing entropy is higher than the melting entropy of the alloy, generally forming a high entropy solid solution phase of a class of alloys.) a substrate coated with hafnium. The bonding mechanism, resistance to high-temperature oxidation, and hardness of the sample tests are carried out. The results show that zirconium in the matrix will diffuse into the hafnium coating during the high-temperature sintering process and form the HfZr alloy transition layer, the coating thickness of the composite is about 120 μm, and the diffusion distance of zirconium in the hafnium coating is about 60 μm, this transition layer chemically combines the hafnium coating and the HEA substrate into a monolithic alloy composite. The results

High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. frame.system: Refractory high‐entropy alloys designed for high-temperature structural applications. The starting state is that these multi-principal element alloys, while offering high strength at extreme temperatures, tend to form non-protective oxide scales under prolonged oxygen exposure.
frame.goal: Improve high‐temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of an adherent, slow-growing, protective oxide scale.
frame.limitation: The alloys’ inherent poor oxidation resistance at high temperatures leads to rapid, non-protective oxide growth.
constraints: must define temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions
improvement must be quantified relative to the untreated alloy
frame.regime: For example, operating around 1200°C in an air atmosphere or oxygen partial pressure equivalent to air, with exposure durations on the order of 100 hours, to simulate extreme service conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous attempts involving multi-element alloying to enhance oxidation resistance have sometimes led to complex phase equilibria without reliably forming a continuous protective oxide scale. Conventional alloying adjustments (e.g., without reactive element additions) have fallen short at these extreme conditions.

decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys focused on tuning the bulk composition to encourage in-situ formation of protective oxides (e.g., formation of CrTaO4-based layers in PMC6513993) even though the results were sensitive to the alloy’s phase stability. Later efforts moved toward surface interventions — for example, the hafnium coating in PMC10488483 demonstrated that a controlled, reactive coating can form a transition zone (HfZr alloy) that effectively limits oxidation. This evolution shows a shift from complex bulk alloying strategies to localized surface treatments aimed at promoting a coherent, adherent oxide scale.
decision.unsolved: Despite the promising results from both composition tuning and coating approaches, a reliable, straightforward intervention that consistently forms an adherent, slow-growing protective oxide scale on refractory HEAs at extreme temperatures (around 1200°C in air for ~100 hours) has not yet been achieved.
decision.lever: Deposition of a thin reactive hafnium coating
decision.why: Building on the promising evidence from coating studies, this single intervention would directly modify the alloy surface by depositing a thin Hf-rich layer that, upon high-temperature exposure, oxidizes to form a protective HfO2-rich scale. This approach leverages the known mechanism of reactive element effects—improving scale adhesion and retarding oxide growth—thus aligning with the observed trend and directly addressing the limitation of non-protective oxide formation without the complications of altering the bulk alloy composition.
